strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered pipeline for building open-source data-analytic agents, covering data synthesis, trajectory filtering, training, and code-based multi-turn rollout.
Introduces DataMind-12K, a high-quality trajectory dataset spanning 18 fine-grained task categories and multiple file formats, with a plan to release data and models.

Proposes useful techniques: recursive easy-to-hard task composition, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling with self-consistency and reflection, dynamic SFT/RL weighting, void-turn filtering, and memory-frugal asynchronous rollout.

Reports strong empirical results: DataMind-14B achieves the best average score (71.16% pass@1) among evaluated proprietary and open-source models, and DataMind-7B is the best open-source model (68.10%).
Provides practical analysis and insights on self-consistency filtering vs. best trajectory selection, SFT/RL tradeoffs via dynamic gamma, and cold-start effects on RL gains.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: code, prompts, hyperparameters, and training/evaluation details are provided, with models and full data promised after review.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: most components (e.g., DAPO, dynamic SFT/RL weighting, self-consistency) are adapted from prior work, so the core contribution is primarily empirical and engineering-oriented.
Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o-mini as a judge for both trajectory filtering and final benchmark scoring, without human validation or reliability analysis of the judge.

The main average improvement over the strongest proprietary baseline DeepSeek-V3.1 is marginal (71.16 vs. 70.58 pass@1) and is driven mainly by BIRD; no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported.

Potential benchmark contamination/leakage is not analyzed: training data includes BIRD/OmniSQL database files while BIRD validation is used for evaluation, and TableBench/DABench overlap with public sources is not checked.

Full ablations on the main benchmarks are missing for several core components (task taxonomy, recursive composition, knowledge augmentation, rule-based filtering, asynchronous rollout, void-turn filtering), and SFT-only/RL-only final scores are not reported.
The data collection pipeline discards files larger than 1,000 rows, which conflicts with the stated goal of handling diverse-format, large-scale data files and limits training coverage.
Baseline comparisons may be incomplete: proprietary models are evaluated only in a zero-shot ReAct setup, and recent general agent-tuning or data-analysis agent methods are not compared.
The claim of being the first to systematically investigate agent post-training scaling in data analysis may be overstated given existing agent training and data-analytic agent literature.
RL training is limited to around 350 steps due to data scarcity, so the scalability and stability claims for the proposed training recipe are not fully demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building generalist open-source data-analytic agents that can handle diverse file formats and multi-step reasoning.
Proposes a comprehensive pipeline covering data collection, task taxonomy, recursive query composition, trajectory synthesis, filtering, hybrid SFT+RL training, and stable multi-turn code rollout.
Curates DataMind-12K, a sizable and diverse trajectory dataset, and trains 7B/14B models that show strong balanced performance across three data-analysis benchmarks.
Includes useful empirical analyses on self-consistency filtering and dynamic SFT/RL weighting, offering potentially actionable insights for agent training.
Provides a reproducibility statement and promises code/data release, with a subset of training data submitted.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol is non-standard and potentially invalid: DABench and TableBench are evaluated with GPT-4o-mini as judge instead of original metrics, TableBench tasks are filtered, and tables are converted to sqlite, making comparisons to prior work and the claimed SOTA unreliable.

The central claim of outperforming proprietary models is overstated: the average gain is narrow and driven mainly by BIRD, while DeepSeek-V3.1 is better on DABench and TableBench; no statistical significance tests or error bars are reported.

Baseline comparison is not fully convincing: proprietary models are evaluated zero-shot with ReAct, while the proposed model benefits from extensive synthesized trajectories and RL, and specialized baselines are trained/evaluated under different settings.

Insufficient ablations: many proposed components (recursive easy-to-hard composition, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling, void-turn filtering, rollout optimizations, dynamic gamma versus standard SFT-then-RL/RL-only) are not isolated, so their individual contributions are unclear.

Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing techniques such as ReAct, DAPO, dynamic SFT/RL weighting, and trajectory filtering in an engineering recipe, without a fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical insight.
Potential data contamination is not addressed: training uses BIRD and OmniSQL training data plus web-scraped files, yet evaluation includes BIRD validation without decontamination checks.
Reproducibility is only partial: full DataMind-12K is not released, only a 3,843-example subset is provided, and model checkpoints are promised only after review.
The claim of being the first to systematically investigate scaling in this scenario is too strong given prior work on agent tuning and synthetic trajectory data.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: building open-source generalist data-analytic agents that can handle diverse file formats and long-horizon multi-step reasoning.

Proposes a comprehensive and well-motivated pipeline, including a fine-grained task taxonomy, recursive easy-to-hard query composition, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling, model/rule-based filtering, dynamic SFT+RL training, and memory-efficient code-based multi-turn rollout.

Curates DataMind-12K, a high-quality trajectory dataset, and trains DataMind-7B/14B models that achieve strong average performance, surpassing both proprietary and open-source baselines on the reported aggregate metric.

Provides useful empirical analyses and insights: self-consistency filtering is non-trivial, SFT loss can both stabilize and destabilize RL training, and RL narrows but does not reverse base-model performance gaps.
Reproducibility effort is reasonably strong: code is submitted, hyperparameters and prompts are detailed, and the authors commit to releasing the full dataset and models after review.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the work primarily integrates existing components (taxonomy, self-consistency filtering, SFT+RL, DAPO, sandboxed rollout) into a data-analytic agent pipeline, with no fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical contribution.

Evaluation is restricted to three benchmarks (DABench, TableBench, BIRD), and the main metric relies on GPT-4o-mini as a judge, which may introduce bias and does not replace rigorous human or rule-based validation. No human evaluation is provided.

The claim of outperforming DeepSeek-V3.1 and GPT-5 is based on average scores; on DABench and TableBench, DeepSeek-V3.1 actually outperforms DataMind-14B, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is overbroad and should be qualified per benchmark.

Baseline comparisons for specialized models such as TableLLM and Table-R1 rely on author reproductions rather than official checkpoints, raising questions about whether these baselines are optimally tuned and fairly compared.

Scale and generalization are limited: only Qwen backbones at 7B/14B are used, RL training runs for only ~350 steps due to data scarcity, and it is unclear whether the recipe scales to larger models or broader task distributions.

During review, only a 3,843-example subset of DataMind-12K is available; full dataset and trained models are withheld until after review, limiting independent verification of the central data contribution.

Presentation and clarity issues remain: Equation 8 is malformed, the paper is dense, and some appendix prompts have formatting errors. Statistical significance or variance across runs is not thoroughly reported.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building open-source generalist data-analytic agents that can handle diverse file formats and long-horizon code-based reasoning.

Provides a complete and reasonably well-described pipeline covering data-file collection, taxonomy-guided query synthesis, recursive easy-to-hard composition, trajectory sampling/filtering, dynamic SFT+RL training, and stable multi-turn rollout.
Releases DATAMIND-12K and the 7B/14B models (or promises release), with detailed hyperparameters and prompts, supporting reproducibility.

Reports strong empirical results across DABench, TableBench, and BIRD, with DATAMIND-14B outperforming several proprietary and open-source baselines and DATAMIND-7B performing best among open-source models.

Includes useful ablations and analyses on data volume, training strategy, self-consistency filtering, SFT/RL weighting, cold-start effects, and judge robustness, yielding actionable insights for agent training.

Engineering contributions for stable multi-turn rollout, such as asynchronous interaction, chunked code maintenance, sandboxing, and memory/time caps, are practical and relevant for scaling agent training.
weaknesses: The main evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o-mini as a judge, and the same judge model is used during training as the answer reward. Although cross-judge and Rouge-L checks are provided, they are limited and do not fully rule out judge bias, reward hacking, or systematic overestimation of DATAMIND.

Proprietary baselines are evaluated only under a zero-shot ReAct-style setup rather than their strongest agent scaffolds, prompting strategies, or fine-tuned variants. This makes the headline claim that DATAMIND outperforms GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3.1 less conclusive.

Specialized open-source baselines such as TableLLM, Table-R1, OmniSQL, and SQL-R1 may be disadvantaged by benchmark conversions, prompt mismatch, and evaluation protocols that differ from their native task formats.

The methodological novelty is largely incremental: the paper combines existing ideas such as ReAct, taxonomy-guided synthesis, self-consistency filtering, SFT+RL, DAPO-style RL, and sandboxed code execution into a large empirical system rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithm or learning paradigm.

The synthesized trajectories are produced by DeepSeek-V3.1, so the trained agents may partly distill that model’s behavior. Contamination analysis is limited to header overlap and does not address semantic or query-level overlap with benchmarks.

Evaluation is limited to three main benchmarks, with QRData only in the appendix and no human evaluation. The paper does not comprehensively compare against concurrent data-analytic agent systems under equal training and inference budgets.

Some training and evaluation choices may favor the proposed method: checkpoint selection based on validation performance after unstable runs, use of the same judge for reward and evaluation, and data synthesis/evaluation both involving GPT-4o-mini.

The scope remains constrained to tabular data and textual questions, with Qwen-family backbones up to 14B and limited RL steps. This limits claims about generalist data-analytic agents and scalability.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: building open-source generalist data-analytic agents that can handle diverse file formats and long-horizon multi-step reasoning.

Provides a comprehensive pipeline covering data collection, taxonomy-guided query synthesis, recursive composition, trajectory sampling/filtering, hybrid SFT+RL training, and multi-turn code rollout optimizations.
Curates and releases DataMind-12K and DataMind-7B/14B models, which could be useful resources for the community if fully released.
Reports strong empirical results on DABench, TableBench, and BIRD, with DataMind-14B claiming an average score above strong proprietary baselines.
Includes several useful ablations: data volume scaling, SFT vs RL vs SFT+RL, self-consistency filtering vs best-trajectory selection, cold-start effects, and judge-model comparison.
Attempts to address potential judge bias via an external judge (Qwen-2.5-72B) and Rouge-L comparisons, and includes a data-contamination overlap analysis.
Provides detailed training and inference hyperparameters, prompts, and implementation details, improving clarity and reproducibility relative to many system papers.
Offers actionable empirical insights about SFT/RL trade-offs and the role of self-consistency filtering in agent training.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the recipe mostly combines existing techniques such as fine-grained taxonomies, self-consistency filtering, DAPO/GRPO-style RL, dynamic SFT+RL weighting, and code-runtime engineering. There is no fundamentally new algorithm or conceptual advance.

The central SOTA claim is not fully convincing: the improvement over DeepSeek-V3.1 is small (71.16 vs 70.58 average pass@1), and DeepSeek-V3.1 is actually stronger on two of the three main benchmarks (DABench and TableBench); the average win is driven mainly by BIRD.

Evaluation protocol deviates substantially from standard benchmark settings: TableBench is filtered and converted, DABench/TableBench are scored with model-as-judge instead of original metrics, and BIRD uses validation plus materialized exact-match evaluation. This makes direct comparisons with prior reported numbers difficult.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently strong: proprietary and open-source models are mostly evaluated zero-shot with ReAct, not with competitive data-analysis scaffolds. Data Interpreter is relegated to the appendix, and its reproduction discrepancy is dismissed rather than fully resolved.

The same GPT-4o-mini judge is used for training-time filtering/reward and main evaluation, creating a potential reward-hacking and evaluation-bias concern. The external-judge and Rouge-L checks are only partial and do not replace the main results.

No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the main results, despite several margins being small; the three-trial pass@1/pass@3 protocol does not establish statistical reliability.

Key pipeline components are not ablated: recursive easy-to-hard composition, task taxonomy, knowledge-augmented sampling, rule-based filtering, reward components, and especially the memory-frugal rollout optimizations are not empirically validated.

Claims about stable training and memory-frugal rollout are largely qualitative; there are no measurements of memory usage, throughput, crash rates, or rollout stability, despite these being listed as core challenges.

The data-contamination analysis only checks header overlap and does not examine row/value/question overlap. Given that BIRD training data and OmniSQL schemas are used for synthesis, stronger contamination controls are needed.

Reproducibility is limited during review: only a 3,843-example subset of DataMind-12K is provided, models are not released until after review, and the pipeline depends on proprietary models (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-4o-mini), making exact reproduction difficult.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially 'new state-of-the-art' and 'outperforming the strongest proprietary baselines' when the gains are marginal, benchmark-dependent, and measured under non-standard protocols.

Clarity issues remain: the reward equation is garbled/unclear in the manuscript, and several analysis conclusions are based on small subsets (e.g., 3,843 training examples and 240 test examples) rather than the full benchmark suite.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building open-source generalist data-analytic agents that can handle diverse file formats and long-horizon code-based reasoning.

Proposes a comprehensive and well-engineered pipeline, including fine-grained task taxonomy, recursive easy-to-hard query synthesis, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling, self-consistency/model-based/rule-based filtering, dynamic SFT+RL training, and stable multi-turn rollout optimizations.

Delivers strong empirical results: DATAMIND-14B achieves the best average score among evaluated models and outperforms strong proprietary baselines such as DeepSeek-V3.1 and GPT-5, while DATAMIND-7B is the best open-source model on the reported benchmarks.

Includes useful ablations and analyses, such as data-scaling behavior, SFT-vs-RL training strategies, self-consistency filtering, judge-model sensitivity, and training stability insights, which add actionable value for the community.

Provides a curated dataset (DATAMIND-12K), promises model/data release, gives detailed training/inference hyperparameters, and includes a data contamination analysis, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
The paper is generally clear, well-structured, and positions itself well within the emerging area of agentic data analysis.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is limited to three benchmarks (DABench, TableBench, BIRD), with additional QRData results only in the appendix; broader validation across more diverse data-analysis tasks, modalities, and file types is still needed.

GPT-4o-mini is used as both the training reward judge and the evaluation judge, which could introduce bias toward the proposed model. The external-judge and Rouge-L checks help mitigate this concern, but they do not fully eliminate it, and Rouge-L is itself a weak metric for answer correctness.

The methodological novelty is more in integration and empirical scaling than in fundamentally new algorithms: the pipeline combines known ideas such as ReAct-style agents, DAPO, self-consistency filtering, and hybrid SFT/RL objectives. This is still valuable, but may be viewed as a system/dataset contribution rather than a deep technical advance.

Some baseline comparisons are not entirely apples-to-apples: proprietary models are evaluated zero-shot with a standard ReAct prompt, while trained baselines are adapted from different task formulations and training corpora. The reported results are encouraging but do not fully isolate the source of gains.

Data contamination is checked mainly via header overlap. While the reported overlap is low, semantic or task-level leakage is not exhaustively quantified, especially since the training pipeline uses sources such as BIRD training data while evaluating on a BIRD split.

Scale is limited: experiments mainly use the Qwen family up to 14B and RL runs to roughly 350 steps. It remains unclear how well the recipe generalizes to larger backbones, longer RL schedules, additional modalities, and other training algorithms.

The full DATAMIND-12K dataset is not available during review due to file-size constraints; only a subset is released in the supplement, which somewhat limits immediate reproducibility until the promised post-review release.
